prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS MACHINES CORP" (ticker IBM), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "IBM", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: International Business Machines Corporation
result.industry: Enterprise software, IT consulting and infrastructure (hybrid cloud and AI)
markets: Hybrid cloud platform software (Red Hat OpenShift, RHEL, Ansible)
Automation, data and AI software (watsonx, HashiCorp, Confluent, Apptio)
Mainframe (IBM Z) and Power servers and storage

mission.statement: At IBM, we are driven by a relentless pursuit of our purpose to be the catalyst that makes the world work better.
mission.plain: IBM wants its technology and know-how to help the world's big organisations run better.

about.plain: IBM makes the computer programs and big, super-reliable computers that banks, airlines and governments use to keep their most important systems running. It also sends experts to help companies plan and build new technology, such as artificial intelligence. It owns Red Hat, which makes software that lets companies run their apps on any cloud. It is also building quantum computers, a new kind of computer that could solve problems today's machines cannot.
about.customers: Large companies and governments, especially banks, insurers, airlines, retailers and telecom firms, in more than 175 countries.
about.everyday: When you pay with a card, take money from an ATM or book a flight, the transaction very often runs on an IBM mainframe in the background.

money.plain: Red Hat cloud software, automation, data and AI tools, mainframe software
experts who plan and build tech and AI projects for clients
mainframes, Power servers, storage and support
loans and leases to help clients buy IBM gear and software
real-time data streaming software bought for about $11 billion in Q1 2026
quantum computers and cloud access to them; fault-tolerant machine targeted for 2029

result.summary: IBM has a real but narrow moat built on switching costs: thousands of the world's largest banks, insurers and governments run core transaction systems on IBM Z mainframes and IBM software that are risky and expensive to replace, and Red Hat gives it a strong position in hybrid cloud. Its advantage is weaker in consulting and commodity hardware, where it competes with Accenture, the hyperscalers and Indian IT firms, and 2026 showed the market fears AI coding tools could erode the mainframe lock-in.

pricingPower.evidence: Gross margin rose every year from 54.0% in 2022 to 58.2% in 2025 as the mix moved to software (44% of 2025 revenue), and the z17 mainframe cycle was running at nearly 130% of the z16 program in Q2 2026 with clients holding 85% of installed MIPS maintaining or growing capacity; but consulting revenue grew only about 2% in 2025 and Q2 2026 GAAP gross margin fell 1.0 point, showing limited power outside the software and mainframe franchise.

moats.evidence: IBM is a 115-year-old trusted brand for mission-critical enterprise IT and holds a large patent portfolio, but the brand no longer signals technical leadership in cloud or AI the way Microsoft, Google or Nvidia do.

Core banking, payments and airline systems written in COBOL over decades run on IBM Z and its transaction-processing software (CICS, IMS, Db2), and migrating them is multi-year and risky; Red Hat Enterprise Linux and OpenShift are also deeply embedded in enterprise data centres.

Red Hat's open-source communities (Linux, Kubernetes, Ansible) and the HashiCorp Terraform ecosystem create some developer and partner network benefits, but IBM's products are not network-effect businesses.

With $67.5B of 2025 revenue, about 264,000 employees and $8.3B of R&D, IBM has global scale in services and R&D, but hyperscalers and Indian IT firms have lower cost structures in cloud and outsourcing.
IBM is effectively the only remaining vendor of high-end mainframes, a niche too small for a new entrant to justify building a rival platform.

IBM's hybrid, multi-cloud and open-source pitch (run anywhere, not locked to one public cloud) is a deliberate contrast to the hyperscalers, but they have largely matched it with Azure Arc, Anthos and AWS Outposts.

Decades of mainframe engineering, chip design (Telum II, Spyre AI accelerator) and running regulated workloads for banks give IBM know-how that is hard to replicate, though consulting know-how is more easily copied.

IBM Research and its quantum team (with a $10B+ five-year quantum investment plan and the planned Anderon quantum foundry backed by $1B of CHIPS incentives) are distinctive assets, but none is truly exclusive.

customers.evidence: Customer loyalty is very high in mainframe and core software (clients representing 85% of installed MIPS were maintaining or growing capacity in Q2 2026), but consulting is more transactional and IBM said in July 2026 that many large deals slipped and it 'did not adapt and move quickly enough'.

talent.evidence: IBM Research remains a respected home for scientists in AI, semiconductors and quantum, but IBM is not seen as a top destination versus the big AI labs and hyperscalers, and repeated job cuts and return-to-office mandates weigh on its employer reputation.

product.evidence: IBM Z is best in class for secure, high-volume transaction processing and Red Hat Enterprise Linux/OpenShift lead in enterprise Linux and hybrid Kubernetes, but its watsonx AI platform and Granite models are niche next to OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google, and its quantum lead (fault-tolerant target 2029) is still unproven commercially.

threats: AI coding agents (e.g. Anthropic's February 2026 COBOL-modernization claims, which triggered IBM's steepest one-day share drop in about 26 years) could make migrating mainframe code off IBM Z much cheaper
Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) absorbing hybrid-cloud and AI platform spending, squeezing Red Hat and watsonx
Generative AI deflating consulting project sizes and pricing; IBM Consulting grew only about 2% in 2025 and was flat in Q2 2026
Execution risk on large acquisitions (HashiCorp $6.4B in 2025, Confluent about $11B in 2026) and a rising debt load of about $62B
Mainframe product-cycle swings: Infrastructure revenue fell 7.4% in Q2 2026 after the z17 launch peak
Quantum computing timelines (fault-tolerant system targeted for 2029) may slip or rivals such as Google could get there first

ceo.name: Arvind Krishna
ceo.background: Electrical engineer: B.Tech from IIT Kanpur and PhD in electrical engineering from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; joined IBM Research in 1990, led the 2019 Red Hat acquisition, CEO since April 2020 and chairman since January 2021

c1.evidence: IBM leads the niche mainframe market and Red Hat leads enterprise Linux/hybrid Kubernetes, and it is a top player in the emerging quantum industry, but it is a follower, not the leader, in the fast-growing AI and public cloud markets.

c2.evidence: Customers choose IBM for trust, security and continuity in mission-critical systems (IBM Z, CICS, Db2) and for Red Hat's open hybrid platform; that lock-in is durable but AI-driven code migration tools threaten to weaken it.

c3.evidence: Almost everyone recognises the IBM name, but ordinary people do not use its products directly and it is no longer seen as the default leader in computing the way Microsoft, Google or Nvidia are.

c4.evidence: IBM states its purpose 'to be the catalyst that makes the world work better' and emphasises hybrid cloud, AI and quantum, but the mission is generic and management messaging centres on free-cash-flow and revenue-growth targets.

c6.evidence: "legacy, reliable, mainframes, Big Blue" are the first words for most people; the impression is respectful but mixed, seeing IBM as dependable and historic rather than innovative.

c7.evidence: IBM sells into the large, growing enterprise AI, hybrid cloud, data and automation markets; its generative AI book of business passed $12.5B by January 2026 and software revenue grew 11% in 2025.

c8.evidence: Quantum computing (fault-tolerant system targeted for 2029, more than $10B planned five-year investment and the Anderon quantum foundry) and AI security (Lightwell, a $5B commitment launched July 2026) are big new markets, but both are unproven commercially.

m1.evidence: Krishna set out a clear hybrid-cloud-plus-AI strategy in 2020, spun off Kyndryl in 2021 and laid out a quantum roadmap to 2029, but his vision follows rather than defines the AI era.

m2.evidence: Krishna is a 35-year IBM lifer who has made long-term bets (Red Hat, HashiCorp, Confluent, quantum), but he is a hired professional manager, not a founder, and owns about 360,000 shares.

m4.evidence: Krishna emphasises client success and skills programmes, but IBM's repeated job cuts and AI-driven back-office replacement plans undercut a servant-leadership image with employees.

m5.evidence: He refocused IBM on software and research-driven products (Telum II and Spyre chips, Granite models, quantum processors), yet the culture is still seen as bureaucratic and slow; Krishna himself wrote in July 2026 that IBM 'did not adapt and move quickly enough'.

m6.evidence: Krishna holds a PhD in electrical engineering from the University of Illinois and spent decades in IBM Research and software engineering before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: Krishna is regarded as a thoughtful, low-key steward who pushes responsible AI, open-source models and skills training, though there is no unusual evidence of purpose beyond running the business well.

m7b.evidence: He gave the 2020 convocation address at IIT Kanpur and was invited to deliver the convocation address at IIM Bangalore, but no commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard or MIT is on record.

m8b.evidence: Krishna is a reserved, technocratic CEO with a low public profile compared with figures like Elon Musk or Alex Karp.

m9.evidence: Under Krishna revenue rose from $55.2B (2020, after Kyndryl) to $67.5B (2025), gross margin from 55.9% to 58.2% and free cash flow to $14.7B in 2025, but growth slowed in Q2 2026 (revenue +1%) and full-year guidance was cut to 4-5% constant currency.

m10.evidence: IBM is cost-disciplined (ongoing productivity programmes, workforce rebalancing, 2025 SG&A of $20.1B on revenue up 8%), but it is not known for a frugal founder-style culture.

c10.evidence: IBM systems quietly process a large share of the world's card payments, bank transactions and airline bookings, improving many lives indirectly, but few people use IBM products directly.

p2.evidence: Building mainframes with near-zero downtime, custom AI chips and quantum processors aimed at a fault-tolerant machine by 2029 is extremely hard and important to global finance and science.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from 2020 to 2025: $55.18B, $57.35B, $60.53B, $61.86B, $62.75B and $67.54B (2020 recast for the Kyndryl spin-off).

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 55.9% in 2020 to 58.2% in 2025 (dipping to 54.0% in 2022) and pre-tax margin rose from 4.7% to 15.3%, but neither rose steadily every year.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 IBM had $62.0B of total debt (including $13.0B of IBM Financing debt) against $8.1B of cash and marketable securities and $13.2B of 2025 operating cash flow; equity was positive at $34.5B.

f4.evidence: Pre-tax income rose from $2.57B in 2020 to $10.33B in 2025, but operating cash flow was flat at $13.93B (2023), $13.45B (2024) and $13.19B (2025).

v1.evidence: IBM Z is clearly the best choice for ultra-reliable, high-volume transaction processing, but in most of IBM's markets (AI, cloud, consulting) it is one of several comparable options.

v2.evidence: IBM is a respected but not top-ranked employer; it does not appear near the top of Glassdoor or Fortune best-places-to-work lists, and repeated layoffs weigh on its reputation.

c5.evidence: If IBM vanished overnight, banks, card networks, airlines and governments running on IBM Z and IBM software would face serious outages, so institutions would miss it badly, though ordinary consumers would not notice directly.
